healthInfo.qualityNotes: Excellent healthcare system with high-quality hospitals, especially in major cities (Rome, Milan, Florence). English is spoken at larger hospitals but less so in smaller clinics. Public healthcare is free or low-cost for residents; tourists can access emergency care at public hospitals.
healthInfo.pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-8pm. Some close for lunch (1-4pm). In large cities, some pharmacies are open 24/7. Look for the green cross sign (Croce Verde). Farmacia turns into a farmaceutico di turno (on-duty pharmacy) after hours for urgent needs.
healthInfo.pharmacyTips: Pharmacies are widely available. Many medications require a prescription. The pharmacist (farmacista) can advise on minor ailments. Some OTC products like ibuprofen and paracetamol are available without prescription.
healthInfo.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require validation by an Italian doctor. Italy has stricter rules than some EU countries — many antibiotics and prescription medications require an Italian prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in Italy. Some codeine products are restricted.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, methylphenidate)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring an Italian prescription or special import authorization from the Ministry of Health.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines (Valium/diazepam, Xanax/alprazolam)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A valid prescription is required. Italy closely monitors these medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal in Italy but heavily restricted to specific conditions and only available through hospital pharmacies.

healthInfo.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English/Italian listing all medications with generic names. Bring sufficient supply for your trip in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry the prescription documentation at all times. EU citizens should carry the EHIC card.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for short stays, but strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC.
travelInsurance.tips: Italy's public hospitals provide emergency care free of charge to all people. For non-emergency care, you'll need travel insurance. Carry your insurance details and a 24/7 emergency contact number. Pharmacies may direct you to a hospital for serious conditions.

recommended: Hepatitis A (for extended stays or close contact with locals)
Meningococcal disease (for students or long-term stays)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

healthInfo.waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Italy. In some southern regions, tap water may have a strong chlorine taste but is safe. Bottled water (acqua minerale) is widely available.
healthInfo.foodSafetyTips: Italy has excellent food safety. Be cautious with raw eggs (mayonnaise, tiramisu) in rural areas. Wild mushrooms (funghi) are popular — only eat those verified by a licensed mycologist. Be cautious with buffalo mozzarella from non-reputable sources. Food in restaurants and tourist areas is very safe.
sources: Italy Ministry of Health (Ministero della Salute)
healthInfo.medicalTourismNote: Italy is known for elective procedures, fertility treatments, and cosmetic surgery tourism, particularly in Milan and Rome.
